title: The Assessment Gap in U.S. Counter-Terrorism Strikes
gist: A former State Department counter-terrorism programs advisor documents that the U.S. government imposes rigorous performance monitoring on $80 million foreign-assistance portfolios while U.S. Africa Command and Southern Command have stopped publishing strike outcome and civilian-harm data entirely — including a maritime campaign that killed at least 221 people across at least 66 strikes and reported zero civilian casualties while admitting it does not positively identify the dead.

insights.claim: The U.S. government demands far more performance evidence from a counter-terrorism grant recipient than from an airstrike, an asymmetry the author treats as the core governance failure rather than a legal necessity.
insights.so_what: Programs that must show results lose funding while kinetic campaigns that show nothing keep it — a budget-allocation bias that favors strike-centric contractors over assistance implementers.
insights.quote: the same government demands far more of a grant recipient than it does of an airstrike
insights.locator: Analyzing Counter-Terrorism Strikes
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Counter-terrorism assistance funding was withheld when a project underperformed or reported late, with baselines set before work started and indicators agreed in advance — a standard that produced legible mixed results rather than no results.
insights.so_what: The measurement template is the benchmark against which the kinetic campaigns fail; Congress could import it, which would be a material compliance cost for strike programs.
insights.quote: None of that money moved without a performance monitoring plan.
insights.locator: For eight years I helped decide
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: A campaign that publishes no outcome data does not produce a disappointing answer — it produces no answer and no way to assess effectiveness, meaning absence of reported failure cannot be read as success.
insights.so_what: Apply the same test to any opaque program you are underwriting: silence is not a null result, it is an unmeasurable one, and it should be priced as maximum uncertainty.
insights.quote: A campaign that publishes no outcome data does not produce a disappointing answer. It produces no answer and no way to assess its effectiveness.
insights.locator: I can tell you where it worked and where it did not
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: The author's entire annual East Africa counter-terrorism portfolio ran about $80 million while Southern Command reported obligating $527.9 million on Operation Southern Spear in a single quarter and $647 million between September 2025 and March 2026.
insights.so_what: The spending has moved roughly an order of magnitude from monitored assistance to unmonitored kinetic operations — follow the appropriations shift when sizing defense versus development exposure.
insights.quote: My entire annual portfolio ran about $80 million. Southern Command reported obligating $527.9 million on Southern Spear in a single quarter, and $647 million between September 2025 and March 2026.
insights.locator: My entire annual portfolio
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Across two combatant commands the United States has stopped producing information on whom strikes hit and how many were killed or injured, and the mechanisms that once produced it lapsed within the past 18 months.
insights.so_what: An 18-month blackout window means no independent party can assess legality or effectiveness — a latent legal and political liability that accumulates until a scandal forces disclosure.
insights.quote: the mechanisms that once produced it have lapsed within the past 18 months
insights.locator: Analyzing Counter-Terrorism Strikes
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Africa Command strike releases degraded from a January 2024 statement naming six al-Shabaab dead near Caad with no civilian harm, to a March 2025 line saying only that enemy combatants were killed, to August 2026 releases carrying only a date, an organization and a distance from the nearest town.
insights.so_what: A documented three-step degradation gives a clean timeline for FOIA litigation and congressional pressure; the trend line, not any single release, is the evidence.
insights.locator: The Reporting That Stopped
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: The identical operations-security caveat appears on both the detailed and the empty Africa Command releases across all three years, proving the security constraint is not what changed.
insights.so_what: This kills the official justification for opacity and makes the policy indefensible in a hearing — a specific vulnerability for the department's public position.
insights.quote: The caveat sits above the detailed and the empty reporting alike. Whatever changed, it was not the security constraint.
insights.locator: The Reporting That Stopped
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Africa Command has left four quarters of civilian harm assessments unpublished from July 2025 through June 2026, precisely the period covering the largest sustained strike campaign in its history.
insights.so_what: The blackout coincides exactly with peak activity — the strongest circumstantial case that the silence is outcome-driven rather than procedural.
insights.quote: The command has left four quarters unpublished, July 2025 through June 2026, covering the largest sustained strike campaign in its history.
insights.locator: The command's own accounting stopped, too.
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: The Section 1057 annual civilian casualty report covering 2025 reached Congress on Aug. 10, 2026, three months past the May 1 statutory deadline, even though the report states its determinations as of Feb. 1, 2026 — six months before delivery, proving analysis was not the bottleneck.
insights.so_what: Demonstrable deliberate delay rather than analytical lag is the hook for conditioning appropriations, the author's proposed remedy.
insights.quote: The assessment was not the holdup.
insights.locator: The mandatory report is separate.
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Congress wrote the civilian casualty accounting requirement for military operations specifically in the FY2018 National Defense Authorization Act and the department has missed it each of the last three years, defeating the objection that grant-world standards are being improperly imported into targeting.
insights.so_what: The obligation is statutory and military-native, so remediation is a compliance question, not a policy debate — raising the odds of eventual forced disclosure.
insights.quote: The department has missed it each of the last three years.
insights.locator: The obvious objection is that this compares
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: The department delivered the unclassified civilian casualty report to members of Congress without releasing it publicly as the statute requires, with CBS News and Stars and Stripes describing obtaining the report rather than receiving it.
insights.so_what: Statutory public-release obligations being quietly ignored without consequence is the pattern to watch; it only breaks when appropriations are conditioned.
insights.quote: CBS News and Stars and Stripes described obtaining the report rather than receiving it.
insights.locator: The same provision requires
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Reported civilian casualties jumped from two killed and two injured in the 2024 report to 153 killed and 243 injured in the 2025 edition, all in Yemen.
insights.so_what: A roughly 75-fold jump in acknowledged civilian deaths concentrated in one country is the kind of number that drives congressional restriction of strike authorities.
insights.quote: The 2025 edition recorded 153 civilians killed and 243 civilians injured, all in Yemen.
insights.locator: The 2024 civilian casualty report
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: The campaign of strikes on vessels in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific has killed no fewer than 221 people across at least 66 strikes and was recorded as producing zero civilian casualties.
insights.so_what: A zero against 221 dead is an auditable impossibility that creates concrete legal exposure for the officials certifying it.
insights.quote: which has killed no fewer than 221 people across at least 66 strikes
insights.locator: The same report recorded no civilian casualties
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Defense officials told Rep. Sara Jacobs they need not positively identify people aboard small craft to strike them, requiring only a connection to a cartel designated as a foreign terrorist organization in 2025 or to an affiliate.
insights.so_what: Targeting by category rather than identification is the legal fault line; it is the specific admission that would anchor any future litigation or authority rollback.
insights.quote: they do not need to positively identify the people aboard the small craft
insights.locator: Representative Sara Jacobs
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: A zero civilian casualty count combined with an admitted inability to identify the dead means the government is classifying by designation rather than by assessment — the zero describes the category assigned before the strike, not a conclusion about who was killed.
insights.so_what: This reframes the statistic from a fact about outcomes into a fact about process, which is the argument that actually moves oversight bodies.
insights.quote: If a vessel’s designation makes everyone aboard a combatant, the zero is not a conclusion about whom the campaign killed.
insights.locator: Those two facts do not reconcile.
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: The 11 people killed in a September 2 strike came from coastal towns on Venezuela's Paria peninsula identified by local media as the country's main human-trafficking hub, and the Joint Staff's Rear Adm. Brian Bennett conceded in a classified briefing that some of the dead could have been trafficking victims.
insights.so_what: A conceded possibility that victims of trafficking were killed as combatants is the specific fact pattern most likely to force a policy reversal.
insights.quote: A trafficking victim is not a member of a designated organization.
insights.locator: A strike on September 2 shows what that standard cannot cover.
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Designating cartels as foreign terrorist organizations in 2025 is the stated basis for striking vessels, meaning the government has treated counter-narcotics as counter-terrorism to obtain killing authority and thereby inherited the counter-terrorism reporting obligation.
insights.so_what: Authority arbitrage cuts both ways: borrowing the CT legal frame imports its disclosure duties, which is the lever oversight can pull.
insights.quote: The government has treated counter-narcotics as counter-terrorism when it wants the authority to kill, and the reporting obligation necessarily follows.
insights.locator: The maritime campaign arrives with different architecture
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Southern Command told the Lead Inspector General it would not publicly release its measures of effectiveness for Operation Southern Spear, whose mission statement is classified along with its target list, strike count and lethal-versus-interdiction decision criteria.
insights.so_what: When a command refuses to disclose even how it measures success, the program has no external falsification mechanism — treat published claims of progress as unverifiable.
insights.quote: Southern Command told the inspector general that it would not publicly release its measures of effectiveness
insights.locator: What U.S. Southern Command Told Its Own Inspector General
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Denied a strike count by Southern Command, the inspector general built one from the New York Times and ABC News — a statutory oversight body reconstructing basic operational facts from journalism.
insights.so_what: Oversight reduced to media scraping is a measurable collapse in the internal control environment; expect it cited in any push to condition funding.
insights.quote: Denied a strike count by the command, the inspector general built one from the New York Times and ABC News.
insights.locator: What U.S. Southern Command Told Its Own Inspector General
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: The only available assessment of whether the maritime campaign reduced narcotics flow was a leaked Drug Enforcement Administration analysis finding no change in cocaine supply or price, while the Southern Command commander testified in March that cartels had adapted by shifting routes and moving to air traffic and shipping containers.
insights.so_what: Unchanged price and supply is the market's own verdict on campaign effectiveness — the cleanest available signal that $647 million bought displacement, not disruption.
insights.quote: finding no change in cocaine supply or price
insights.locator: That leaves one measurable question
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: High-profile attacks in Mogadishu rose from 10 in 2015 to 18 in 2016 to 42 in 2017, including an October truck bomb that killed 587 people, after which donor-funded fixed and mobile vehicle checkpoints stopped a repeat attempt in December 2019 at the city's western edge.
insights.so_what: A documented before-and-after with a specific defeated attack is what a measured program can show and an unmeasured one cannot — the standard of evidence to demand.
insights.quote: it runs to 10 in 2015, 18 in 2016, and 42 in 2017
insights.locator: I should be straight about what all that measurement produced.
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: A countering violent extremism program encouraged or assisted more than 1,200 defectors to leave al-Shabaab between 2020 and 2024, while outside Mogadishu al-Shabaab was never contained and is arguably stronger now.
insights.so_what: The honest mixed verdict is the point: measured programs can admit partial failure, which is what makes their successes credible.
insights.quote: Mogadishu stopped burning at the scale it once had.
insights.locator: Defeat of al-Shabaab was never the standard.
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Counter-terrorism assistance should be evaluated the way fire protection is — sensors and alarms, a response capability, and prevention to reduce sparks — rather than against the standard of defeating the adversary.
insights.so_what: A reusable evaluation frame for any risk-mitigation spend: judge detection, response and prevention separately instead of against total elimination of the threat.
insights.quote: We build counter-terrorism assistance the way we build fire protection
insights.locator: Defeat of al-Shabaab was never the standard.
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: A 2020 State Department Inspector General inspection found one employee serving as grant or agreement officer representative for 86 projects worth almost $147 million, a span of control flagged as beyond what the bureau could properly oversee.
insights.so_what: Even the model compliance regime had severe capacity failures — but they were documented, which is the author's entire distinction between a failing system and an unknowable one.
insights.quote: The difference is that somebody wrote it down.
insights.locator: Nor was it self-administered.
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

themes.theme: The case for silence, and its limits

insights.claim: Detailed battle damage disclosure carries real risks — revealing sources, methods and patterns of life, and letting groups like al-Shabaab and the Islamic State debunk named-kill claims with recordings — yet the quarterly civilian harm reports ran 22 consecutive editions without any cited operational security incident.
insights.so_what: The empirical record defeats the theoretical objection; 22 clean editions is the number that makes restoring publication politically cheap.
insights.quote: The quarterly civilian harm reports ran for 22 consecutive editions without an adverse operational security disclosure incident anyone has cited.
insights.locator: The Case for Silence
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Nigeria's Defence Headquarters published on May 19, 2026 that a joint operation eliminated 175 Islamic State fighters, named three commanders killed and listed what was destroyed, while Africa Command never published its own assessment of the same operation.
insights.so_what: A partner government facing identical propaganda risk chose disclosure — which removes the last structural excuse and creates a comparative embarrassment lever for Congress.
insights.quote: the only public accounting of an American operation came from a partner government
insights.locator: Nigeria published what Washington would not.
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Federal law requires the Secretary of State to transmit an annual terrorism report by April 30 covering the prior calendar year, but the most recent edition released May 1, 2026 covered 2024 — satisfying a different year's requirement rather than being merely late.
insights.so_what: A whole reporting year has silently disappeared; the distinction between late and skipped matters for whether statutory remedies are available.
insights.quote: It satisfies that of a different year.
insights.locator: This pattern extends beyond the Pentagon.
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Officials under both this administration and the last have missed the terrorism report deadline without consequence, so the author argues Congress should condition appropriation on the reporting it already requires.
insights.so_what: The proposed remedy — appropriations conditionality — is the specific legislative vehicle to watch in the next NDAA or approps cycle.
insights.quote: Congress could condition appropriation on the reporting it already requires.
insights.locator: Restoring the Record
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks

insights.claim: Civilian deaths in airstrikes can radicalize individuals with no prior affiliation with the targeted group, an observation attributed to Viktor Marsai of the Soufan Center, meaning unreported civilian harm compounds the threat it is meant to reduce.
insights.so_what: The second-order effect means opaque strike campaigns may be net-negative on the threat metric they are funded against — a case for structurally underestimating their returns.
insights.locator: The Case for Silence
insights.speaker: Jim Loucks
